Git backup and surviving a Gitea outage

The repo carries the application code. It no longer carries the per-device source of truth: that was retired from git on 2026-08-05 and now lives in the content-addressed store under data/sot/ (live harvest in data/reports/) — see source-of-truth-spec.md and metrics-architecture.md. Because it sits inside data/, it is replicated to the standby by satom-ha-datasync and carried in the backup bundles, with no git involvement at any point.

The git remote is therefore a distribution point for code — not a custody point for anything. This document is about what happens when it is not there, and about the artifact that makes that survivable.

What breaks when Gitea is down

Nothing in the request path. Only two commands in the whole codebase talk to the remote: self_update.py (git fetch) and git_service.git_publish (git push). Everything else — the UI, device management, device_sync, pg_dump bundles, the appliance pushes to {backup-server}, the HA rsync — is unaffected.

Function Effect while the remote is unreachable
Software Update & HA git fetch fails → no code update and no code rollback
Firmware SoT manifest unreadable (the .out binaries live on {backup-server}, so pulls still work)
Reconciler (AUTO) cannot fetch → drift is not reconciled
Sync Prod blocked — the dev repo is the source
requirements.txt bump after a pip change the pin is not persisted; the next code update reverts the library

No data is lost during the outage. The commits pile up locally and push themselves when the remote returns.

The dangerous part is the return, not the outage

deploy/self_update_runner.py rewrites the checkout with:

git reset --hard origin/<branch>

Any commit that exists here and not on the remote becomes unreachable and is eventually garbage-collected. With the reconciler in AUTO (its default), that can fire on its own the moment Gitea comes back and reports behind > 0.

What would be gone is local code history — a hotfix committed here while the remote was unreachable. Device config history is no longer at risk on this path: it lives in data/sot/, which git reset --hard does not touch and which the diff/history/restore views in System Backup & Restore read directly.

The guard

Before the reset the runner now calls preserve_local_commits():

  • local commits not on the target → refs/backup/pre-reset-<UTC stamp>
  • a dirty worktree → git stash create (builds a commit object without touching the index or worktree) → refs/backup/pre-reset-<stamp>-dirty

Refs are never pruned, so git log refs/backup/pre-reset-… recovers everything. If the commits cannot be parked, the update aborts — a deferred update beats silent history loss. A failure to stash a dirty tree is reported but not fatal: reports/ is dirty in normal operation and regenerates on the next sync.

The System Backup page lists any refs/backup/* that exist.

The alert

ahead > 0, behind == 0 — the exact signature of a failing push — used to fire nothing: git.diverged requires behind > 0 and git.behind requires behind > 25. The new git.ahead_unpushed keys off age, not count (one commit stuck for three days is worse than twenty in the last hour):

  • warning once the oldest unpushed commit passes alerts.git_ahead_max_hours (default 6 h, Settings → Alerts → "Git unpushed max")
  • critical at 8× that threshold

The artifact: git bundle

app/services/git_backup.py writes a git bundle — one file holding the whole history and every ref (--all, which includes the refs/backup/* safety refs). It is verifiable offline (git bundle verify) and clonable directly. No server, no daemon, no credentials embedded.

Delta-compressed it is a few MB (the 208 MB .git on disk is mostly unreachable objects and old packs), so retention is cheap — default 7 per node.

Where the copies land

Copy Location How it gets there
this node data/git-bundles/ the button / the git_bundle automation
standby same path satom-ha-datasync mirrors data/ every 5 min
off-rack {backup-server} <system_path>/git/ SFTP push (default on)
operator your laptop the download button

{backup-server} is a separate failure domain on purpose: Gitea and the standby both live on {hypervisor}, so a {hypervisor} outage takes copies 2 and 3 offline together. {backup-server} is on {hypervisor}, the primary on {hypervisor}.

reports/ and .git are deliberately not in the HA rsync. The standby has its own git checkout; rsyncing reports/ over it would leave its worktree dirty and break its own reset --hard. The bundle is the correct vehicle for that history, and it goes further off-box than the rsync does.

Using it

# integrity, before trusting a copy
sha256sum satom-repo-<ts>.bundle       # compare with the value shown in the UI
git bundle verify satom-repo-<ts>.bundle

# total loss: rebuild from the bundle alone
git clone satom-repo-<ts>.bundle satom

# selective: pull the rescued history into an existing checkout
git fetch satom-repo-<ts>.bundle '+refs/*:refs/recovered/*'
git log refs/recovered/backup/pre-reset-<stamp>

Operational notes

  • Deletes are primary-only: satom-ha-datasync rsyncs data/ with --delete, so a bundle deleted on the standby comes back within 5 min.
  • Schedule it with the git_bundle action in Automation (params.push_server defaults to the saved setting).
  • Take one by hand before any update while the remote is unreachable — that is precisely when the local commits exist nowhere else.

Related

  • docs/privilege-model.md — the app runs as satom; the bundle is written by the web worker, not by the privileged runner.
  • docs/encryption-and-node-tls.md — the origin remote rides HTTPS.
